noteRef.subtopicTitle: Enthalpy of Solution - Ionic Charge & Radius

specPoints.text: understand the effect of ionic charge and ionic radius on the values of enthalpy change of hydration and the lattice energy of an ionic compound

primer.text: Lattice and hydration enthalpies both track charge density. Larger ions spread charge further apart and weaken attraction, so lattice energies grow less exothermic down a group; higher charges pull harder and make them more exothermic. The same logic makes small, highly charged ions hydrate most exothermically, as fluoride and magnesium illustrate.

lessons.title: Charge and radius rule the lattice
lessons.opening: Two dials set a lattice energy: ionic charge and ionic radius. Bigger ions hold their charge further apart, weakening attraction and softening the value - caesium fluoride is gentler than potassium fluoride. Higher charges pull harder and deepen the value - calcium oxide outdoes potassium chloride on charge alone.
keyPoints: Lattice energy depends on two key factors: the charge and the radius of the ions that build the crystalline lattice.
Lattice energy becomes less exothermic as ionic radius increases: charge spreads out, ions sit further apart, and attractions weaken.
Caesium fluoride's lattice energy is less exothermic than potassium fluoride's, because the larger Cs+ ion weakens the Cs+-F- attraction.
Lattice energy becomes more exothermic as ionic charge increases, since higher charge density strengthens the electrostatic attraction.
Calcium oxide's lattice energy is more exothermic than potassium chloride's: 2+ with 2- beats 1+ with 1-, and the smaller Ca2+ and O2- ions add to the effect.

low.restatement: Bigger ions soften lattice energy; higher charges deepen it; attraction runs centre to centre, so distance matters.
low.analogy: Magnets on long rods: slide them further apart and the pull fades; swap in stronger magnets and the pull returns.
low.examPointer: Compare like with like: same anion, different cation - then the difference is the cation's.

medium.restatement: Electrostatics scales with charge and falls with separation, so every lattice is a compromise between how charged and how crowded its ions are.
medium.analogy: Street lamps: brighter bulbs (charge) light further, but every extra metre of distance dims the glow.
medium.examPointer: The centre-to-centre detail explains why radius, not just charge, enters the argument.

check.stem: As ionic radius increases, lattice energy becomes

options.text: Less exothermic, as the charges sit further apart and attract more weakly

options.explanation: That is the charge trend, not the radius trend.

check.stem: Caesium fluoride's lattice energy is less exothermic than potassium fluoride's because

options.text: The Cs+ ion is larger than K+, weakening the attraction to fluoride
options.explanation: Same anion, bigger cation, softer value.
The anion is identical in both.

check.stem: As ionic charge increases, lattice energy becomes

options.text: More exothermic, because higher charge density strengthens the attractions

options.explanation: Formation from gaseous ions always releases energy.

check.stem: Calcium oxide's lattice energy is more exothermic than potassium chloride's because

options.text: The 2+/2- charges attract far more strongly than 1+/1-, and the smaller ions sit closer
options.explanation: Both levers point the same way.

check.stem: The attraction between lattice ions acts between

options.text: The centres of the ions, so larger ions mean larger centre-to-centre distances
options.explanation: The centre-to-centre framing is why radius matters.
The centre framing is the model.
The whole ion's charge is the model.

check.stem: State the two key factors affecting lattice energy.
check.modelAnswer: The charge and the radius of the ions making up the crystalline lattice.

check.stem: State the lattice-energy comparison between CsF and KF with the reason.
check.modelAnswer: CsF is less exothermic than KF, because Cs+ is larger than K+, weakening the attraction to F-.

check.stem: Explain why higher ionic charge makes lattice energy more exothermic.
check.modelAnswer: Electrostatic attraction grows with the product of the charges, so doubling each ion's charge quadruples the pull; a stronger attraction releases more energy as the lattice forms.

check.stem: Predict which is more exothermic: NaF or NaCl, and justify.
check.modelAnswer: NaF: the fluoride ion is smaller than chloride, so the Na+ to anion centre-to-centre distance shrinks and the attraction strengthens, deepening the lattice energy.

lessons.title: The same logic for hydration
lessons.opening: Hydration enthalpies obey the same charge-density logic from the water's side. Small or highly charged ions attract water molecules hardest, so their values are most negative: fluoride beats chloride, and magnesium beats barium among the 2+ ions.
keyPoints: Hydration enthalpies are exothermic because energy is released as water molecules bond to the ions.
Negative ions attract the delta-positive hydrogens of water; positive ions attract the delta-negative oxygen.
Greater charge density brings a greater hydration enthalpy: smaller ions or larger charges pull water in more strongly.
Fluoride carries a more negative hydration enthalpy than chloride; Mg2+ carries a more negative one than Ba2+.

low.restatement: Charge density governs hydration: small or highly charged ions hydrate most exothermically - F- over Cl-, Mg2+ over Ba2+.
low.analogy: A gripping hand: smaller fingers with a firmer squeeze hold the water molecules tighter.
low.examPointer: Mirror the lattice lesson: same lever, different partner - water instead of the lattice.

medium.restatement: Water's delta charges seek the ion's pull, and the pull scales with charge density; the tighter the grip, the deeper the energy release.
medium.analogy: Velcro: more hooks per inch (charge density) grips harder.
medium.examPointer: Group comparisons down a group soften the value; across a charge jump deepen it.

options.text: Energy is released as water molecules bond to the ions

options.explanation: Water is the solvent, not a reactant consumed.
Ions do not shrink on hydrating.

check.stem: The ion feature that most strengthens hydration is

options.text: High charge density - a small radius or a large charge
options.explanation: Both raise the pull on water.

options.text: A full outer shell of electrons

check.stem: Fluoride's hydration enthalpy is more negative than chloride's because

options.text: The smaller F- ion attracts water molecules more strongly
options.explanation: Charge density falls down the group.
It attracts it, just less strongly.

check.stem: Mg2+ hydrates more exothermically than Ba2+ because

options.text: Mg2+ is smaller, so its charge density and grip on water are greater

check.stem: Within the ion-dipole picture, the water's hydrogens face

options.text: Negative ions, attracted to their delta-positive charge
options.explanation: The oxygen end faces the positive ions.
The oxygen end takes that job.

check.stem: State the hydration comparison between F- and Cl-.
check.modelAnswer: Fluoride's hydration enthalpy is more negative than chloride's, since the smaller ion attracts water more strongly.

check.stem: State the hydration comparison between Mg2+ and Ba2+.
check.modelAnswer: Mg2+ has the more negative hydration enthalpy, as its higher charge density grips water more tightly.

check.stem: Explain why charge density controls hydration enthalpy.
check.modelAnswer: Hydration releases energy in proportion to the ion's pull on water's delta charges; that pull strengthens with concentrated charge - small radius, high charge - so charge density is the controlling quantity.

check.stem: Predict which hydrates more exothermically, Li+ or K+, and state the trend across Group 1.
check.modelAnswer: Li+: the smallest Group 1 cation grips water hardest, and hydration enthalpies grow less negative descending the group as radii swell.

glossary.definition: An ion's charge concentrated by its size, the controlling quantity for lattice and hydration enthalpies.
The force between oppositely charged ions, growing with charge and shrinking with distance.
The grip between an ion and water's delta charges that releases hydration energy.
